summary: Defines a profile of SASL for POP3, letting a client pick an authentication mechanism, run an exchange, and optionally negotiate a security layer. It consolidates POP3 AUTH information into one document and replaces RFC 1734. It is on the standards track.

eli5.summary: A way to prove who you are to your mailbox before it hands over your mail.

subtitle: How a POP3 client logs in using any SASL mechanism, with the AUTH command and the SASL capability.

tldr.problem: POP3 authentication was spread over several documents, and the older AUTH command predated SASL and was unclear about initial client responses.
tldr.mechanism: The server lists mechanisms in the SASL capability. The client sends AUTH with a mechanism name and optional Base64 initial response, then answers challenges, optionally negotiating a security layer.
tldr.outcome: RFC 5034 replaces RFC 1734, updates RFC 2449, and requires clients and servers to implement PLAIN over TLS.

today: RFC 5034 is a Proposed Standard that obsoletes RFC 1734 and updates RFC 2449. The unit metadata lists no later RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why POP3 AUTH Was Rewritten
sections.content:
The POP3 AUTH command from RFC 1734 had problems. It resembled the SASL framework but pre-dated it, so it lacked pieces such as a way to list the available mechanisms. RFC 2449 added the CAPA command and an initial client response, but how that response should be handled stayed unclear.

A full implementation needed material from at least five documents. This RFC combines RFC 1734 and RFC 2449, clarifies them, and updates them where needed. It obsoletes RFC 1734 and updates Section 6.3 of RFC 2449.
sections.eli5: The login rules were scattered across many papers. This one puts them all in a single place and fixes the confusing parts.

sections.title: The SASL Capability
sections.content:
A server announces support with the SASL tag in its CAPA response. The argument is a space-separated list of the SASL mechanisms it supports. The capability adds the AUTH command, which is valid only in the AUTHORIZATION state.

If a server does not support CAPA or does not advertise SASL, clients SHOULD NOT try AUTH. If they do, they MUST NOT send an initial response, for compatibility with RFC 1734.

The list may change after a successful STLS. Servers MUST keep including the SASL capability even after a successful AUTH, though no further AUTH commands may be issued.
sections.eli5: The client first asks the mailbox which ways of proving identity it accepts, and picks one from the list.

sections.title: The AUTH Command
sections.content:
The form is AUTH mechanism [initial-response]. The server then runs a series of challenges and responses specific to that mechanism. A challenge is a line with +, a space and Base64 text. A client response is a Base64 line. The client can cancel by sending a line with a single *, and the server MUST then reply with -ERR.

The initial response saves a round trip. If it is omitted and the mechanism needs one, the server sends an empty challenge, a line with only + and a space. A zero-length initial response is sent as a single =. The 255-octet command limit from RFC 2449 still applies, so if the response would make the command too long, the client MUST NOT use the parameter.

On success the server sends +OK and the session enters the TRANSACTION state. If the exchange fails, the server MUST reject with -ERR and behave as if no AUTH had been issued, and the client may try again. Base64 must be strictly checked: invalid characters or misplaced pad characters MUST be rejected.
sections.eli5: It is like a secret-word game: the mailbox asks, you answer, and when you get it right the door opens. You can also quit the game by sending a star.

sections.title: Security Layers, Identities and Required Mechanisms
sections.content:
The authorization identity is a simple username and SHOULD be prepared with the SASLprep profile of StringPrep. If preparation fails or gives an empty string (unless sent as empty), the server MUST fail the authentication.

If a security layer is negotiated, it starts right after the final client response for the client and right after the success reply for the server. Each side MUST then discard knowledge obtained before, such as the list of POP3 extensions. When both TLS and a SASL layer are active, TLS encoding is applied after SASL encoding when sending. The SASL service name is pop.

Client and server implementations MUST implement the PLAIN mechanism running over TLS. A server MUST support a configuration that does not advertise or permit plaintext password mechanisms unless STLS has negotiated TLS, and this SHOULD be the default. Clients MUST verify the TLS server certificate, and both sides SHOULD implement mechanisms that avoid plaintext passwords, such as GSSAPI. The RFC's own Security Considerations section says only that issues are discussed throughout the document.
sections.eli5: Passwords should only travel inside a locked tube, which is what TLS gives. The mailbox must be able to refuse plain passwords outside of it.

sections.title: Formal Syntax and Examples
sections.content:
The syntax uses ABNF. The auth-command rule is AUTH SP sasl-mech [SP initial-response] followed by optional lines of Base64 and an optional cancel line, *. The continue-req rule is + SP [base64] CRLF, and it is added to the response rule from RFC 2449. Strings are case-insensitive, and implementations MUST accept them that way.

The examples show three flows: AUTH PLAIN with an initial response after STLS, AUTH PLAIN without it using an empty challenge, and DIGEST-MD5, where the server begins with a challenge.
sections.eli5: The exact grammar says precisely which lines are allowed, so every mail program writes them the same way.

sections.title: What Changed From RFC 1734 and RFC 2449
sections.content:
The RFC lists nine changes. References were updated, particularly to RFC 4422. The SASL-based semantics from RFC 2449 are now normative. The handling of initial client responses is defined with examples. A new minimum requires TLS plus PLAIN.

Further changes say that SASLprep SHOULD prepare authorization identities, that TLS encoding goes after SASL encoding, that the mechanism list can change after STLS, that = means a zero-length initial response, and that POP3 does not allow extra data with +OK. The IANA section says the POP3 extension and GSSAPI service name registries were updated to point to this RFC instead of RFC 1734.
sections.eli5: The new rules fix unclear spots in the old ones and add a rule that everyone must at least support one safe way to log in.
